title: Mexico Saves 159.35 Billion Pesos in Debt Interest Payments Through September
author: Dora Villanueva
content:
_This article by[Dora
Villanueva](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Dora%20Villanueva) originally
appeared in the [November 2, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/11/02/economia/ahorro-
de-159-mil-350-mdp-en-pago-de-intereses-de-la-deuda-a-septiembre), Mexico's
premier left wing daily newspaper._

Interest payments on the public debt were **159.35 billion pesos lower than
programmed through September** , owing to the appreciation of the Mexican
currency, better interest-rate conditions and the refinancing operations
themselves, the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit (SHCP) reported.

The ministry had projected that through September it would have disbursed
1.118 trillion pesos in payments on the public debt, but only **958.9997
billion** were paid.

![Chart: Mexico's projected vs. actual interest payments on public debt,
January–September 2026](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/mexico-debt-interest-savings-chart.png)Chart: Mexico
Solidarity Media, with data from the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit
(SHCP).

According to the Finance Ministry and private financial firms, these savings
in the financial cost of the public debt largely explain the containment of
the public deficit, including that of entities under indirect budgetary
control.

That gap between revenue and spending was expected to be around 1.2117
trillion pesos through September, but it ended at 959.582 billion. Víctor
Gómez Ayala, chief economist at Finamex, highlighted that **two-thirds of the
difference is due to the financial cost of the public debt**.

> This lower spending contributed to the better performance of the budget
> balance and to easing the pressures on public finances.
>
> Ministry of Finance and Public Credit

The Finance Ministry made the point when releasing its reports on the state of
the economy and public finances through September.

Interest payments on the debt not only came in below projections, they also
saw **an annual reduction of 3.7 percent in real terms** compared with the
amount spent in the January–September period of last year, the ministry
reported.

BBVA agrees that the financial cost favored the public balance. However, “the
limited fiscal space makes it difficult to continue advancing significantly in
the fiscal consolidation the country requires to stabilize the historical
balance of the public sector borrowing requirements (SHRFSP)” as a percentage
of gross domestic product (GDP), “and to avoid the loss of investment grade.”

As of September, the SHRFSP—the broadest measure of the public debt—reached
19.554 trillion pesos, 976.3676 billion more than in December 2025. However,
as a percentage of GDP, it **remains at 52.6 percent**.

In this regard, Arnulfo Rodríguez, chief economist for Mexico at BBVA, warned
that a tax reform that increases tax collection by at least two percentage
points of GDP will be necessary, given the little margin in public spending
and the expected continued support for Petróleos Mexicanos.

“The proposal is to prioritize a tax reform with measures that improve
compliance and broaden the base of both taxable products and taxpayers. The
aim is that higher collection does not depend on an increase in tax rates and
that it improves the sustainability of public finances,” he explained.
